titleZh: 同样一间客房，为什么退房与续住不能按同一工作量排班？
titleEn: Why Shouldn’t Checkout and Stayover Rooms Count as the Same Workload?
summaryZh: 退房与续住的清扫任务和交付条件不同，同样间数不等于同样负荷。用五行班次观察表核查房型、实际类别、等待、支援、质量和返工，再调整现有班次任务；不照搬论文分钟，不用于削人或个人定额。假设填写示例只演示字段怎样衔接。
summaryEn: Checkout and stayover rooms can involve different cleaning tasks and handover conditions. Use a five-line observation sheet to record actual cleaning categories, waiting time, support, inspections and rework before adjusting room attendant assignments. This article draws on a 2021 single-hotel study without turning its findings into time quotas or staffing conclusions.
contentZh:
同样一间客房，为什么退房与续住不能按同一工作量排班？

因为两类房间的清扫任务和交付条件不同，客房排班应先按本店的房型、清扫类别及实际作业条件识别工作，再分配间数；同样间数不等于同样负荷，不能把快慢差异先归给员工。

Aguilar-Escobar等人在2021年的一项西班牙单店研究中，把客房清扫区分为退房、续住和续住换床品。研究结果显示，房型和清扫类别在该样本内与清扫用时有关。它不能回答另一家酒店“每人应当分多少间”，却能提示管理者：间数不是完整的工作量口径。

为什么退房与续住不能用同一把尺

研究酒店对三类的定义不同。退房清扫是客人离店后，把房间准备给下一位新客；续住清扫服务的是当天仍要使用原房间的客人；续住换床品则另有床品更换事项。其他酒店未必采用同样的服务分类，但分派工作前，仍要问清这批房间各自需要完成哪些事项。

因此，退房与续住的差别，不是给两类房贴一个固定时间标签，而是看房间交给谁、实际要完成哪些事项，以及何时能够进房。计算客房清扫工作量时，也不能把一早列出的计划类别直接当作当天实际工作。

这项研究在一家拥有74间客房的四星级酒店开展，共观察74次清扫，涉及8名员工，其中退房36次、续住35次、续住换床品3次。研究记录房内清扫任务，也记录与清扫直接相关的部分房外工作；但明确不包含员工的其他工作，也没有评价清洁质量。续住换床品只有3次，更不适合据此设一个独立权重。

这些边界决定了论文能怎么用。可以用它检查本店是否漏看任务，不能照搬其分钟数作为个人定额，也不能从有限样本推出培训无效、质量已经下降或人员可以削减。观察中没有测到的内容，不应被排班表补写成结论。

客房排班表怎样看见间数以外的工作

一间房从“列入清扫”到“完成交付”，可能遇到计划类别变化、客人尚未离开、取消清扫、补充物资、设施异常、报修沟通或返工。它们的原因和处理责任不同，不能全塞进“清扫慢”一项。

要把客房服务员的班次分得合理，不能只看每人负责多少间。客房负责人可在本店既有记录上补充几组信息：房型与区域、计划及实际清扫类别、正常作业起止时间、等待与中断、额外事项及原因、物资与跨岗支持、返回与交接、检查结果与返工原因。

计时用于比较任务和发现障碍，不是把员工的每次停顿变成处罚依据。观察前，应由有权限的管理者明确目的、范围、记录人和使用方式，依本店人事制度及适用要求完成必要告知与授权，不在工作表或公开材料中写入可识别的客人、员工资料。无法准确计时的事项如实留空并说明，不补造数字。

还要注意，清扫计时不是完整班次。跨区移动、取送物资、等待进房、设备故障、支援其他工作，都可能影响当班负荷；等待进房也不等于员工可以真正休息。把这些事项另列，才能分清哪些是房内方法问题，哪些是现场条件和协作问题。

一张五行观察表，先用于一个真实班次

本店班次任务观察表

观察范围：日期、班次、楼层或区域、记录人及必要授权，不填住客个人信息。
计划任务：房型与计划清扫类别、对应间数、预计进房条件。
实际过程：实际清扫类别、作业起止、等待中断、额外事项及原因。
支持与质量：补给及跨岗协助、异常处理、检查结果、返工原因与完成状态。
复核与调整：同类任务组合是否合适、哪些必须拆开、哪些事项要交上级决定。

以下是一条假设填写示例，只演示各栏怎样衔接，不对应任何真实酒店、员工或经营结果，也不用于设定工作量标准。

观察范围：某工作日早班，同一楼层的同类房型。
计划任务：首班前根据当时已有的预计信息，将一间房按续住清扫排入既定区域。
实际过程：到房时进房条件尚未确认，先记下等待及原因；与前台核实客人已提前离店且可以进房后，将续住清扫改为退房清扫，不把这段等待改写成房内作业耗时。
支持与质量：按原有楼层安排取得补给，依本店现行项目完成检查；发现的遗漏已经返工并复查，结果如实记录。
复核与调整：班后将这次临时改类及等待列入复盘，下一次分派前先核对当日的预计退房、续住和临时变更，并明确类别变化时向谁确认。是否重新组合相邻任务，要看其他正常班次是否也出现同类情况，不从这一间房推算权重。

汇总时，只先比较同类房型、同类清扫和相近工作条件。若实际类别或条件不同，先解释差异，不急着算员工名次。单日子类样本太少时，只记录现象，不设稳定的分钟权重，更不要把缺失数据补成平均值。

总经理可以授权客房负责人选择一个现有班次观察。首班开始前，先用当时已经掌握的信息按现行办法分工，不等待观察表给出尚不存在的结果。前台提供预计退房、续住及影响进房条件的信息，客房部核对本店服务和交付要求，工程说明已知的影响清扫及安全事项；分派保留既有的楼层熟悉度、质量责任和协作安排。

首班按上述已知安排执行并如实记录，不为凑样本干扰住客或制造额外服务。观察沿用本店现行清洁和检查标准，不另造一套“试点合格线”。遇到安全或质量问题，以及超出既定授权范围的异常，按现行规定即时处理，不能为了完成观察而延到班后。

班后，客房负责人再与相关岗位复核计划与实际类别的差别、等待和中断、支持与返工、实际收尾及房态交接。只有记录能够解释任务或条件差别，才把它用于下一次分派；需要调整时，先处理已经查明的等待、补给或交接问题，而不是机械地将退房与续住一比一交换。单个异常应及时处理，但不能从一间房给此后所有班次设定权重。

哪些情况要停下来，哪些结论不能提前下

若发生检查遗漏、应返工而未返工、异常房交接不清，或实际负荷超出既有安排，先按现行规定纠正；问题未消除前，暂停受影响的后续安排，恢复经确认可行的分工并查明原因。房间尚未达到本店交付条件时，不能用排班“优化”掩盖缺口，更不能据此自动增加可售房。

某班快，也可能是任务较简单、房间状态不同或支援更多；某班慢，也可能是等待离房、设施异常或额外服务占用时间。短期观察不能自动证明人员可以减少。反过来，若在同类任务、相近条件下持续出现明显差异，才进一步检查作业方法、物资支持和培训需要，不能把“任务构成重要”误读成“人的因素永远不重要”。

度假酒店、商务酒店、全服务与有限服务酒店的服务内容不同；同一酒店遇到团队抵店、集中退房或设备异常，也不能机械套用普通班次的观察结果。本方法只解决现有班次的任务识别和分配，不替代编制、收益或筹开放量决定。

下次排班前，先选一个真实班次，把“多少间”还原成“哪些任务、什么条件、谁提供支持”。迈创兄弟C&T（MarvelBros C&T）建议，先看清工作，再决定怎样分配。

资料来源：Aguilar-Escobar等，《Hotel Room Cleaning: Time Study and Analysis of Influential Variables in a Spanish Hotel》，Journal of Industrial Engineering and Management，2021，14(3)，645—660。https://doi.org/10.3926/jiem.3441
contentEn:
Why Shouldn’t Checkout and Stayover Rooms Count as the Same Workload?

The two types of rooms require different cleaning tasks and have different conditions for handing the room over. Room attendant scheduling should therefore first identify the work according to the hotel’s room types, cleaning categories and actual working conditions, and then allocate rooms. The same number of rooms does not necessarily mean the same workload, and differences in speed should not initially be attributed to employees.

In a 2021 study of a single hotel in Spain, Aguilar-Escobar et al. classified room cleaning as checkout, stayover, or stayover with changes, meaning a linen change. The study found that room type and cleaning category were associated with cleaning time within this sample. It cannot tell another hotel how many rooms each person should be assigned, but it does suggest to managers that room count is not a complete measure of workload.

Why Checkout and Stayover Rooms Should Not Be Measured Against the Same Yardstick

The study hotel defined the three cleaning categories differently. Checkout cleaning takes place after a guest has departed and prepares the room for the next new guest. Stayover cleaning serves guests who will continue to use the same room that day. Stayover with changes also involves changing the bed linen. Other hotels may not use the same service categories, but before assigning the work, they still need to establish what tasks each room in the batch requires.

The difference between checkout and stayover rooms is therefore not a matter of attaching a fixed time label to each category. It depends on who will use the room next, what tasks must actually be completed, and when the room can be entered. When calculating the workload for room cleaning, the planned categories listed early that morning cannot simply be treated as the actual work performed during the day.

This study was conducted at a four-star hotel with 74 rooms. It observed 74 cleaning sessions involving a total of 8 employees: 36 checkouts, 35 stayovers, and 3 stayovers with changes. The study recorded cleaning tasks inside the rooms and some work outside the rooms directly related to cleaning. It explicitly excluded other work performed by the employees and did not assess cleaning quality. With only 3 observations of stayovers with changes, this category is particularly unsuitable for setting a separate weighting.

These boundaries determine how the paper can be used. It can help identify tasks that a hotel may have overlooked. Its time figures should not be copied as individual quotas, nor should its limited sample be used to conclude that training is ineffective, that quality has declined, or that staffing can be reduced. Matters not measured during the observations should not be written into the schedule as if they were established conclusions.

How Room Attendant Scheduling Can Reveal Work Beyond Room Counts

Between a room being scheduled for cleaning and its completion for handover, the planned category may change, guests may not yet have departed, cleaning may be cancelled, supplies may need replenishing, facilities may be faulty, maintenance needs may have to be communicated, or rework may be required. These events have different causes and responsibilities and cannot all be placed under “slow cleaning.”

To allocate work sensibly among room attendants, look beyond the number of rooms assigned to each person. The head of housekeeping could add several groups of information to the hotel’s existing records: room type and work area; planned and actual cleaning categories; the start and end of the normal cleaning work; waiting time and interruptions; additional tasks and their reasons; supplies and support from other roles; returns and handovers; inspection results and reasons for rework.

Timing is for comparing tasks and identifying obstacles, not for turning every pause an employee takes into grounds for a penalty. Before observation begins, an authorised manager should specify the purpose, scope, person responsible for recording, and how the information will be used. Necessary notice and authorisation should be completed in accordance with the hotel’s personnel policies and applicable requirements. Information that could identify individual guests or employees should not be included in worksheets or public materials. Where an item cannot be timed accurately, it should be left blank with an honest explanation, rather than filled in with a fabricated figure.

Cleaning time is also not the whole shift. Moving between areas, collecting and delivering supplies, waiting to enter rooms, equipment failures and supporting other work may all affect the employee’s workload during the shift. Waiting to enter a room does not necessarily mean that an employee can actually rest. Listing these items separately helps distinguish issues with the cleaning method inside the room from issues with on-site conditions or coordination between roles.

Start with One Actual Shift and a Five-Line Observation Sheet

Hotel Shift Task Observation Sheet

Scope of observation: Date, shift, floor or area, person recording and necessary authorisation. Do not enter guests’ personal information.
Planned tasks: Room types and planned cleaning categories, corresponding number of rooms, and expected conditions for entering the rooms.
Actual process: Actual cleaning categories, the start and end of the work, waiting time and interruptions, and additional tasks and their reasons.
Support and quality: Supplies and assistance from other roles, how irregularities were handled, inspection results, reasons for rework and completion status.
Review and adjustment: Whether similar tasks are appropriately grouped, which tasks must be separated, and which matters need to be escalated for a decision.

The following is a hypothetical completed example. It demonstrates only how the fields connect. It does not represent any real hotel, employee or operating result, and it is not intended to set a workload standard.

Scope of observation: A morning shift on a weekday, covering the same room types on the same floor.
Planned tasks: Before the shift began, one room was scheduled as a stayover cleaning within an established area based on the projected information available at the time.
Actual process: When the room attendant reached the room, the conditions for entering it had not yet been confirmed. The wait and its reason were recorded first. After the front desk confirmed that the guest had departed early and that the room could be entered, the category was changed from stayover to checkout cleaning. The waiting period was therefore recorded separately, rather than as time spent cleaning inside the room.
Support and quality: Supplies were obtained through the existing arrangements for the floor, and the inspection was completed according to the hotel’s current inspection items. The omission identified was reworked and then checked again, with the outcome recorded accurately.
Review and adjustment: After the shift, this last-minute change of category and the wait were included in the review. Before the next assignment of work, the day’s projected checkouts, stayovers and last-minute changes should be checked, together with the person to approach for confirmation when a category changes. Whether adjacent tasks should be grouped differently depends on whether other comparable, normally operating shifts show the same pattern; a weighting should not be inferred from this one room.

In the initial summary, compare only rooms of the same type, the same cleaning category and broadly similar working conditions. If the actual categories or conditions differ, explain the difference first rather than rushing to rank employees. If the sample for a subcategory on a single day is too small, record only the observation. Do not establish a stable weighting in minutes, let alone fill missing data with an average.

The general manager can authorise the head of housekeeping to select an existing shift for observation. Before the first observed shift begins, the work should be allocated using the information already available and the hotel’s current methods, without waiting for the observation sheet to produce results that do not yet exist. The front desk provides information on projected checkouts, stayovers and anything affecting the conditions for room entry. Housekeeping checks the hotel’s service and handover requirements, and engineering explains known matters that may affect cleaning or safety. The assignments preserve existing arrangements for floor familiarity, accountability for quality and coordination between roles.

The first observed shift proceeds under the existing arrangements as described above, with a truthful record of what happens. Guests are not disturbed and additional services are not created simply to increase the sample. The observation continues to use the hotel’s current cleaning and inspection standards and does not create a separate “pilot pass mark.” Safety or quality issues and irregularities that fall outside the established scope of authority must be handled immediately under existing procedures and must not be postponed until after the shift to complete the observation.

After the shift, the head of housekeeping reviews with the relevant roles the differences between planned and actual categories, waiting time and interruptions, support and rework, the actual wrap-up and room-status handovers. Only where the records can explain differences in tasks or conditions should they inform the next assignment of work. If an adjustment is needed, address the identified problems with waiting, supplies or handovers first, rather than mechanically exchanging one checkout for one stayover. An isolated irregularity should be dealt with promptly, but one room cannot provide a weighting for every subsequent shift.

When to Stop and Which Conclusions Not to Draw Prematurely

If an inspection is omitted, necessary rework is left undone, the handover of a room with an irregularity is unclear, or the actual workload exceeds what the existing arrangements can accommodate, the situation should first be corrected under current procedures. Until the issue has been resolved, subsequent arrangements affected by it should be paused. Work should return to an allocation confirmed to be practical, and the cause should be identified. When a room does not yet meet the hotel’s handover requirements, scheduling “optimisation” must not be used to conceal the gap, nor should this automatically make additional rooms available for sale.

A faster shift may involve simpler tasks, rooms in a different condition or more support; a slower shift may involve waiting for guests to vacate, facility-related problems or additional services taking up time. Short-term observation does not automatically demonstrate that staffing can be reduced. Conversely, only where clear differences continue to occur for similar tasks under similar conditions should the working methods, supplies support and training needs be examined further. Recognising that the mix of tasks matters must not be mistaken for saying that people-related factors never matter.

Resort, business, full-service and limited-service hotels provide different services. A hotel experiencing group arrivals, a concentration of checkouts or equipment irregularities should not mechanically apply observations from an ordinary shift. This method addresses only task identification and allocation within existing shifts; it does not replace decisions on staffing levels, revenue or the phased release of rooms during a pre-opening period.

Before the next round of scheduling, select one actual shift and go beyond “how many rooms” to identify which tasks are involved, under what conditions, and who provides support. MarvelBros C&T recommends looking at the work clearly before deciding how to allocate it.

Source: Aguilar-Escobar et al., “Hotel Room Cleaning: Time Study and Analysis of Influential Variables in a Spanish Hotel,” Journal of Industrial Engineering and Management, 2021, 14(3), pp. 645–660. https://doi.org/10.3926/jiem.3441
author: 迈创兄弟C&T（MarvelBros C&T）
